title: Quantitative Comparison Strategy
weightage: Very High — roughly a third to a half of every GRE Quant section is Quantitative Comparison
intro: Quantitative Comparison (QC) is the GRE’s signature question type, and it is unlike anything on other tests. You are shown two quantities — Quantity A and Quantity B — and asked only which is larger, not to compute either one exactly. The four answer choices are always the same, in the same order, on every QC question, so you can memorise them once and never re-read them. The winning mindset is comparison, not calculation: you rarely need a final value, just the relationship. That opens up fast tactics — simplifying both columns in parallel, testing a few well-chosen numbers, and recognising when a relationship can flip (which forces the "cannot be determined" answer). This chapter drills the four-choice framework and the three techniques that solve the overwhelming majority of QC questions on test day.

items.name: Choice D
items.formula: the relationship cannot be determined from the information given

items.name: Add / subtract the same amount from both
Multiply / divide both by the same POSITIVE number
Multiply / divide both by a NEGATIVE number

topics.name: The Four Answer Choices
topics.details: Every Quantitative Comparison question offers the identical four choices in the identical order, so learn them once: (A) Quantity A is greater; (B) Quantity B is greater; (C) the two quantities are equal; (D) the relationship cannot be determined from the information given. The single most useful consequence of this fixed menu is a rule about choice D: if both quantities are specific numbers, the answer can never be D. Two fixed numbers always have a definite relationship — one is bigger, or they are equal — so D is only ever correct when the quantities contain variables that can take more than one relationship. That instantly collapses your options: on a purely numeric QC, you are choosing among A, B and C only. Conversely, the moment a variable appears with no full restriction on its value, D leaps onto your radar. Anchoring to these choices before you compute keeps you comparing rather than needlessly solving.

solved.problem: Quantity A: 3² + 4². Quantity B: (3 + 4)². Which choice is correct?
solved.solution: Quantity A = 9 + 16 = 25. Quantity B = 7² = 49. Both are fixed numbers, so D is impossible. 25 < 49, so Choice B (Quantity B is greater).

solved.problem: Quantity A: 25% of 80. Quantity B: 80% of 25. Which choice?
solved.solution: A = 0.25 × 80 = 20. B = 0.80 × 25 = 20. Both fixed and equal, so Choice C. (This uses x% of y = y% of x.)

solved.problem: x is a real number. Quantity A: x². Quantity B: x. Which choice?
solved.solution: Try x = 2: A = 4 > 2 = B. Try x = 1/2: A = 1/4 < 1/2 = B. The relationship changes with x, and x is unrestricted, so Choice D — cannot be determined.

solved.problem: Quantity A: the number of prime numbers between 1 and 10. Quantity B: 4. Which choice?
solved.solution: Primes between 1 and 10 are 2, 3, 5, 7 — that is 4 of them. Both quantities are fixed numbers and equal, so Choice C.

unsolved.problem: Quantity A: 2³. Quantity B: 3². Which choice?
hints: Compute both — they are fixed numbers, so D is out.

unsolved.problem: Quantity A: 1/2 + 1/3. Quantity B: 5/6. Which choice?
n is any integer. Quantity A: n. Quantity B: n². Can this be pinned down?
hints: Test n = 3, then n = 0, then n = 1.

unsolved.problem: Quantity A: 0.2 × 0.2. Quantity B: 0.2. Which choice?
hints: Both are fixed, so not D.
Multiplying by a number below 1 shrinks it.

unsolved.problem: Quantity A: the average of 10, 20 and 30. Quantity B: 20. Which choice?
hints: Both fixed, so D is impossible.

topics.name: Simplify Both Columns Equally
topics.details: Because you only need the relationship, you may treat a QC like a balance scale and perform the same operation on both quantities without changing which side is heavier — provided the operation is legal. You can add or subtract the same amount from both, and you can multiply or divide both by the same positive number, all without touching the comparison. This lets you strip away shared clutter: cancel a common term, clear a denominator, or subtract a value that appears on both sides, until the comparison becomes obvious. The one rule you must never break: multiplying or dividing both quantities by a negative number flips the inequality, and because a variable might be negative, you generally avoid multiplying both sides by an unknown whose sign you do not know. Squaring both sides is only safe when you know both quantities are non-negative. Used carefully, simplification turns a scary-looking comparison into a one-line answer.

solved.problem: Quantity A: 7x + 5. Quantity B: 7x + 9. Which choice?
solved.solution: Subtract 7x from both (legal, and it removes the unknown): Quantity A becomes 5, Quantity B becomes 9. 5 < 9 regardless of x, so Choice B.

solved.problem: Quantity A: (3/4) × 88. Quantity B: (2/3) × 88. Which choice?
solved.solution: Divide both by 88 (a positive number, legal): compare 3/4 with 2/3. Cross-multiply: 3×3 = 9 versus 2×4 = 8, so 3/4 > 2/3. Choice A.

solved.problem: a > 0. Quantity A: a + 12. Quantity B: a + 15. Which choice?
solved.solution: Subtract a from both: 12 versus 15. 12 < 15 no matter what positive a is, so Choice B. (The value of a is a red herring.)

solved.problem: Quantity A: 5⁴. Quantity B: 4⁵. Which choice?
solved.solution: No shared factor to cancel, so compute: 5⁴ = 625, 4⁵ = 1024. Both fixed, and 625 < 1024, so Choice B. (When nothing cancels, the basic calculator or direct computation settles it.)

unsolved.problem: Quantity A: 4x + 7. Quantity B: 4x + 2. Which choice?
Quantity A: (5/6) × 120. Quantity B: (4/5) × 120. Which choice?
y > 0. Quantity A: 3y. Quantity B: 3y − 4. Which choice?
Quantity A: 2⁶. Quantity B: 6². Which choice?
Quantity A: n/5 + 3. Quantity B: n/5 − 1. Which choice?

topics.name: Plug In Smart Numbers (0, 1, negatives, fractions)
topics.details: When a QC contains variables, the fastest route is often to test values rather than manipulate symbols. The art is choosing smart numbers — the ones that expose how a relationship can change. A reliable kit is 0, 1, a negative, and a proper fraction between 0 and 1, because each behaves unusually: zero collapses products, one is the multiplicative identity, negatives flip inequalities and reverse under multiplication, and fractions between 0 and 1 get smaller when squared and larger when you take their reciprocal. Here is the decisive logic: if two different legal test values give two different relationships (once A wins, once B wins), the answer must be D — you have proved it cannot be pinned down. If every value you try gives the same relationship, that is strong evidence for A, B or C, and you can usually confirm it algebraically. Always respect the constraints printed above the quantities: only plug in values the problem actually allows.

solved.problem: x is a nonzero number. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: x³. Which choice?
solved.solution: Try x = 2: A = 2, B = 8, so B wins. Try x = 1/2: A = 0.5, B = 0.125, so A wins. Two different relationships from allowed values means Choice D.

solved.problem: x > 1. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: x². Which choice?
solved.solution: For any x > 1, squaring makes it bigger: try x = 2 (2 vs 4, B) and x = 10 (10 vs 100, B). The constraint x > 1 rules out the fraction case, so Quantity B is always greater — Choice B.

solved.problem: 0 < x < 1. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: √x. Which choice?
solved.solution: A proper fraction’s square root is larger than the fraction. Try x = 1/4: A = 1/4, B = √(1/4) = 1/2, so B wins. Try x = 0.81: A = 0.81, B = 0.9, B wins. Consistent, so Choice B.

solved.problem: a and b are integers with a < b. Quantity A: a + b. Quantity B: ab. Which choice?
solved.solution: Try a = 1, b = 2: A = 3, B = 2, A wins. Try a = 3, b = 4: A = 7, B = 12, B wins. Different relationships, so Choice D.

unsolved.problem: x is any real number. Quantity A: x². Quantity B: x³. Which choice?
hints: Try x = 2, then x = 1/2, then x = −1.
When it flips, the answer is D.

unsolved.problem: 0 < x < 1. Quantity A: 1/x. Quantity B: 1. Which choice?
hints: The reciprocal of a proper fraction exceeds 1.

unsolved.problem: n is a negative integer. Quantity A: n. Quantity B: n². Which choice?
0 < x < 1. Quantity A: x². Quantity B: x. Which choice?
hints: Squaring a proper fraction shrinks it.

unsolved.problem: x is any real number. Quantity A: x + 2. Quantity B: 2x. Which choice?
hints: Set them equal: x + 2 = 2x gives x = 2.
Try x = 1 (A wins) and x = 3 (B wins).

topics.name: When the Answer is "Cannot Be Determined"
topics.details: Choice D — "the relationship cannot be determined" — is the choice test-takers most often get wrong in both directions: they pick it out of laziness, or they miss it when it is genuinely correct. Two clear rules cut through the confusion. First, D is impossible whenever both quantities reduce to specific numbers; fixed numbers always have a definite order, so if you have computed both and they are just numbers, cross D off. Second, D is correct exactly when you can produce two allowed scenarios that give opposite relationships — one where A is bigger and one where B is bigger (or one equal and one not). Proving D therefore means finding a single counterexample to "always A" and a single counterexample to "always B". The usual triggers are unrestricted variables, especially those that could be negative, zero or fractional, and geometry figures that are not drawn to scale (the GRE warns you not to trust the picture). When you see a free variable, actively try to break a tentative answer before committing.

solved.problem: x is a real number. Quantity A: x². Quantity B: 4. Which choice?
solved.solution: Try x = 3: A = 9 > 4, A wins. Try x = 1: A = 1 < 4, B wins. Two opposite outcomes from allowed values, so Choice D.

solved.problem: A rectangle has area 24. Quantity A: its perimeter. Quantity B: 20. Which choice?
solved.solution: Area 24 fixes the product of the sides, not the sides themselves. A 4×6 rectangle has perimeter 2(4+6) = 20 (equal to B). A 2×12 rectangle has perimeter 2(2+12) = 28 (> 20). Different relationships, so Choice D.

solved.problem: x < 0. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: 1/x. Which choice?
solved.solution: For any negative x, both x and 1/x are negative. Try x = −2: A = −2, B = −0.5, so B > A. Try x = −0.5: A = −0.5, B = −2, so A > B. Opposite outcomes, so Choice D.

solved.problem: x and y are positive with x + y = 10. Quantity A: xy. Quantity B: 24. Which choice?
solved.solution: The product varies: x = 5, y = 5 gives xy = 25 > 24 (A wins); x = 2, y = 8 gives xy = 16 < 24 (B wins). Two outcomes, so Choice D.

unsolved.problem: x is a real number. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: |x|. Which choice?
hints: For negatives, |x| is bigger; for positives, equal.

unsolved.problem: The product of two integers is 12. Quantity A: their sum. Quantity B: 7. Which choice?
x² = 49. Quantity A: x. Quantity B: 5. Which choice?
hints: The square root has two signs.

unsolved.problem: A triangle has two sides of length 5 and 8 (figure not to scale). Quantity A: the third side. Quantity B: 10. Which choice?
hints: The third side lies strictly between 3 and 13.

unsolved.problem: Quantity A: 3 + 8. Quantity B: 12 − 1. Which choice? (Watch the trap.)
hints: These are fixed numbers, so D is impossible.

shortcuts: Memorise the four choices once: A greater / B greater / equal / cannot be determined. Never re-read them.
If both quantities are plain numbers, cross off D immediately — fixed numbers always have a definite order.
Treat the comparison like a scale: add or subtract the same thing from both sides, or multiply/divide both by the same POSITIVE number, freely.
Cancel shared terms before computing — often the variable drops out and the answer falls out in one line.
When variables appear, test 0, 1, a negative and a fraction between 0 and 1 — the values that expose flips.
Two allowed test values giving opposite relationships PROVES the answer is D. Stop as soon as you find them.
GRE geometry figures are "not drawn to scale" — reason from the given measurements, never from how the picture looks.
mistakes: Picking D when both quantities are specific numbers (D is then impossible).
Multiplying or dividing both quantities by a variable whose sign is unknown — a negative flips the inequality.
Testing only easy positive integers and missing the flip that 0, a negative or a fraction would reveal.
Squaring both sides when a quantity could be negative, breaking the comparison.
Trusting a not-to-scale figure’s appearance instead of the labelled measurements.
Fully computing each quantity when cancelling a shared term would answer the question far faster.

pyq.q: A QC shows two purely numeric quantities. Can the answer be D?
pyq.a: No. Two specific numbers always have a fixed relationship, so D is off the table — choose among A, B and C.

pyq.q: When is choice D the correct answer?
pyq.a: Exactly when you can find two allowed scenarios giving opposite relationships. One counterexample to "always A" plus one to "always B" proves D.

pyq.q: Quantity A: x²; Quantity B: x, with no restriction on x. What is the answer and why?
pyq.a: D. x = 2 makes A bigger; x = 1/2 makes B bigger. The unrestricted variable lets the relationship flip.

pyq.q: A GRE geometry QC gives a figure "not drawn to scale". How should you treat the picture?
pyq.a: As a rough sketch only. Use the stated measurements and properties; if the unstated parts can vary, the answer is often D.

pyq.q: Is it safe to multiply both quantities by x to clear a fraction in a QC?
pyq.a: Only if you know x is positive. If x could be negative the inequality flips, and if x could be 0 the move is invalid — so usually avoid it.

summary: The four QC choices are fixed and ordered — memorise them so you can compare, not re-read.
If both quantities are specific numbers, the answer is never D; choose A, B or C.
Simplify both quantities in parallel: add/subtract equally, or multiply/divide by the same positive number, to strip shared clutter.
Never multiply both sides by an unknown that could be negative — the inequality would flip.
For variable QCs, plug in 0, 1, a negative and a fraction; these expose relationship flips.
The answer is D exactly when two allowed values yield opposite relationships — find one counterexample each way.
Treat GRE figures as not to scale; reason from the given measurements, and lean toward D when unstated parts can vary.
